hints: Start from the stem clue - the mixture changes from white to colourless. What does white tell you about light passing through at the start?
Link what the enzyme makes to solubility and light transmission, and think why following this change continuously for 100 s tells you about rate.
walkthrough:
What the colour change means**
Think with me about the starting mixture. A 2% protein solution looks white and cloudy, so it scatters and absorbs a lot of light and gives a high absorbance reading of about $1.3$. Neutrase is a protease, so it breaks peptide bonds and converts large insoluble protein molecules into small soluble peptides and amino acids.

Why absorbance tracks activity**
As those soluble products form, the solution clears and becomes colourless. That means less light is absorbed and more is transmitted, so absorbance falls. A faster fall means higher enzyme activity. Measuring for 100 s is long enough to see the progress clearly, for example the control falls from $1.3$ to about $0.2$, so you can compare rates between tubes.

Final answer: Neutrase hydrolyses protein to soluble peptides / amino acids, so cloudiness decreases and more light is transmitted / absorbance falls. The fall in absorbance over 100 s shows the progress / rate of reaction.

hints: Compare each curve to tube D (water control) at the same time, for example at 100 s. Which tubes stay high and which fall low?
Look at A versus B. Both contain copper sulfate but at different concentrations. What does the difference between $0.05$ and $0.01 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ tell you?
Look at C versus D. Both fall together to about $0.2$. What does that tell you about potassium sulfate compared to water?
For explanations, think about inhibitors binding to the enzyme and stopping enzyme-substrate complexes forming, and decide which salt acts this way.
walkthrough:
Describe copper sulfate - strong inhibition**
Read across at the same time. At 100 s, D (water, no inhibitor) has fallen to about $0.2$, showing full activity. A ($0.05 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ copper sulfate) stays high at about $1.25$ to $1.3$, so almost no hydrolysis has happened. That is a large decrease in activity.

Describe concentration effect and potassium sulfate control**
Now compare A and B. B ($0.01 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ copper sulfate) stays near $1.2$ until about 70 s then falls to about $0.9$ at 100 s. So the low concentration inhibits less than the high concentration. C ($0.01 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ potassium sulfate) follows D almost exactly, both reaching about $0.18$ to $0.20$ at 100 s, so potassium sulfate has little or no effect.

Explain in terms of inhibition**
Copper ions act as an inhibitor of Neutrase. They bind to the enzyme, which can change the shape of the active site. Then the protein substrate cannot fit and enter the active site, so enzyme-substrate complexes do not form and protein is not hydrolysed, hence absorbance stays high. Potassium sulfate does not bind in this way, so it is not an inhibitor and the reaction proceeds normally.

Final answer: Copper sulfate decreases Neutrase activity, with $0.05 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ having a greater effect than $0.01 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$; potassium sulfate has little / no effect. E.g. at 100 s absorbance is about $1.25$ in A, $0.9$ in B, but about $0.2$ in both C and D. Copper sulfate acts as an inhibitor by binding to Neutrase so substrate cannot enter the active site / enzyme-substrate complexes do not form; potassium sulfate is not an inhibitor.

hints: If the enzyme is trapped in alginate beads, think about what happens at the end of one batch - do you lose the enzyme with the product?
Think about the food product itself. Why would a customer and manufacturer prefer no enzyme protein mixed into the food?
Think about stability and continuous use. How does fixing the enzyme in place help with yield over time and tolerance of conditions?
walkthrough:
Reuse and recovery**
Free enzyme in solution is lost with the product and cannot be easily got back. When trapped in alginate, the beads can be filtered off or kept in a column while substrate flows past. So the same Neutrase can be used again and again, which raises overall yield and lowers cost.

Clean product**
Because the enzyme stays in the beads, it does not contaminate the food product. That means less purification is needed afterwards, so downstream processing is easier and cheaper, which matters a lot in the food industry.

Stability**
Fixing the enzyme often makes its tertiary structure more stable and less likely to denature by heat or pH change, and it can have a longer shelf-life. It can also reduce product inhibition if product is washed away continuously, keeping the rate high.

Final answer: Enzyme can be easily recovered and re-used, giving higher productivity / yield; product is not contaminated so downstream processing is easier; enzyme is more stable / less likely to denature with longer shelf-life.
